name: Anatolian Rock
about: Anadolu rock grew out of the Istanbul beat scene of the mid-1960s, when bands who had been covering the Shadows began setting Turkish folk songs to electric instruments. By 1970 the formula was settled: the bağlama and its microtonal scales alongside fuzz guitar and organ, Anatolian rhythms in 9/8 and 10/8, and lyrics drawn from the Alevi poets or the political left. Cem Karaca was its conscience, Barış Manço its showman, Erkin Koray its wildest guitarist, and Moğollar the band that gave it a manifesto. Selda Bağcan and Edip Akbayram carried the protest strain through the 1970s until the 1980 coup drove Karaca into exile and the scene underground. Since 2016 Altın Gün, Gaye Su Akyol and Derya Yıldırım have revived it for a worldwide audience.

artists.name: Erkin Koray
artists.why: the father of Turkish rock guitar

artists.name: Edip Akbayram
artists.why: the voice of Alevi protest rock

albums.title: Elektronik Türküler
albums.why: Koray's masterpiece sets Anatolian folk tunes to electric bağlama, fuzz and tape delay across the fifteen-minute 'Cemalim'; the one Turkish rock record everyone agrees on.
Manço's science-fiction concept album with Kurtalan Ekspres, mixing Moog, saz and prog-rock suites; the most ambitious record of the scene's peak.

albums.title: Anadolu Pop
albums.why: Moğollar's manifesto record, cut in Paris and awarded the Académie Charles Cros Grand Prix du Disque: folk themes over a rock rhythm section, mostly instrumental.

albums.title: Nem Kaldı
albums.why: Karaca with Dervişan at the height of his political period, singing folk ballads and workers' songs over heavy, organ-led Anatolian rock.

albums.title: Selda
albums.why: Fuzz guitar, saz and Selda's cutting voice on protest songs about poverty and prison; the Finders Keepers reissue made it a sampling source and a cult classic.

albums.title: Erkin Koray
albums.why: Koray's first LP collects the early-1970s singles that invented Turkish rock; raw, melodic and unmistakable from the first fuzz note.

albums.title: Parka
albums.why: The follow-up sharpened both the politics and the arrangements, with longer suites and a harder rock edge; Karaca at his most urgent.

albums.title: Nedir Ne Değildir?
albums.why: Akbayram and Dostlar at their peak, Alevi folk songs and leftist verse given a thick, fuzzy rock treatment; his finest album.

albums.title: Hürel Arşiv
albums.why: The Hürel brothers' first LP gathers their singles, with Feridun's three-necked guitar pointing at a heavier, prog-leaning Anatolian rock.

albums.title: Not Defterimden
albums.why: Kızılok's gentle, melancholy record of acoustic folk rock, a singer-songwriter's album in a scene of bands; quietly one of the most loved Turkish LPs.

albums.title: Yeni Bir Gün
albums.why: Manço's late-1970s pop turn with Kurtalan Ekspres, lighter than 2023 but full of hits; the point where Anatolian rock became mainstream Turkish pop.

albums.title: Benimle Oynar mısın
albums.why: Ortaçgil's debut is the Turkish singer-songwriter album, acoustic guitar and plain lyrics; it sold nothing in 1974 and has been treasured ever since.

albums.title: Türküz Türkü Çağırırız
albums.why: Mazhar and Fuat's harmony-folk take on Anatolian songs, closer to Simon and Garfunkel than to Koray; the softer side of the movement.

albums.title: Gençlik İle Elele
albums.why: Özkent's instrumental funk arrangements of folk tunes, with Moog, clavinet and breakbeats; rediscovered by Finders Keepers and sampled widely.

albums.title: Oyun Havaları
albums.why: Dilek's electric arrangements of dance tunes with drum machines and fuzz saz; the wedding-band end of Anatolian rock, and oddly hypnotic.

albums.title: Turkish Freakout: Psych-Folk Singles 1969-80
albums.why: The Bouzouki Joe compilation of 45s that introduced many Westerners to the genre; well chosen, with the fuzzier and funkier bands to the fore.

albums.title: Uzelli Psychedelic Anadolu
albums.why: The Uzelli label's own survey of its 1970s catalogue, drawn from master tapes and full of singles that had never been reissued.

albums.title: Duble Oryantal
albums.why: BaBa ZuLa's dub-soaked Istanbul psychedelia mixed by Mad Professor, with electric saz and darbuka; the record that linked the old scene to the new.

albums.title: Gece
albums.why: Altın Gün's Grammy-nominated second record, a Dutch-Turkish band covering Anatolian songs with disco bass and synths; the revival's commercial peak.

albums.title: Hologram İmparatorluğu
albums.why: Akyol's second album, surf guitar and Anatolian scales under a voice modelled on Selda and Müzeyyen Senar; the most original of the new wave.

albums.title: Kar Yağar
albums.why: Derya Yıldırım's bağlama and voice with a Franco-German band on a record that treats the old songs with care and real groove.

albums.title: On
albums.why: The debut that started the revival, a note-for-note affection for Koray and Manço arranged for a dance floor; slighter than Gece but fresh.

albums.title: İstikrarlı Hayal Hakikattir
albums.why: Akyol's third record, darker and more rock-driven, with a political undertow; the best of her albums so far.

albums.title: Zaman Zaman
albums.why: Kızılok's post-coup return, quiet songs for a quieted country; a cult favourite among the singer-songwriters who followed him.

note: Much of the classic era was issued on singles and compiled later, so dates follow the first LP release.
